newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine bids to dampen Chernobyl-danger suggestion.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine bids to dampen Chernobyl-danger suggestion.

text.p: Ukraine sought on Thursday to dampen suggestions that the "tomb" around the Chernobyl power station's ruined fourth reactor posed a serious danger, with a senior official denying a chain reaction had occurred inside.

Volodymyr Horbulyn, secretary of the Security Council, said Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko had spoken out of turn by stating that increased readings of neutron activity last week indicated a nuclear chain reaction within the structure.

"I believe Mr Kostenko is mistaken. He is no specialist in nuclear energy," Horbulyn told a news conference. "Neither he nor I were there when all this occurred. I am inclined to be less pessimistic about what is happening in the sarcophagus."

But Horbulyn, who helped develop nuclear missile launchers in Soviet Ukraine, said the cracking "sarcophagus" remained the single biggest threat facing the former Soviet republic 10 years after the Chernobyl disaster.
"We have to approach this as the biggest threat in Ukraine today -- ensuring the safety of the fourth reactor," he said.
Kostenko himself backtracked in a new statement, saying that news reports had exaggerated the dangers. Even if any further nuclear reaction occurred, he said, it would necessarily be limited.
"All reactors at the station are under the constant supervision of specialists and meet the strictest standards," the official Ukrinform news agency quoted him as saying.
"Even if an emergency situation develops it would not occur beyond the limits of the Chernobyl (30-km exclusion) zone."
Other experts rushed to issue statements playing down the potential consequences of the readings. But they have stressed that the sarcophagus needed replacing -- with Western help.
"The conditions are not present for a thermal explosion," Viktor Baryakhtar, Vice-President of the Academy of Sciences, told Interfax Ukraine news agency.
"Things inside there are so spread around so it is most unlikely. But I cannot guarantee that this won't happen."
Ukrainian officials have said that rain seeping through some of the 1,000 square metres (10,000 sq ft) of cracks in the tomb pushed up readings of neutron radiation by several times last week.
But Western experts have said that the levels are still far below those required to produce an explosion.
